lead: Biomechanical measurement turns body force, foot pressure and limb position into numbers. A pedobarograph maps pressure under the foot. Gait analysis times the walk cycle and measures step and stride. Limb position sensors record joint angle, and velocity and acceleration are obtained from these signals or from inertial sensors. Clinics use these numbers to fit insoles, check recovery after injury and design prostheses. Some syllabi call the whole area biomechanics measurement. The same ideas appear in sports labs and in any instrument that must show how a body moves, not just how its nerves and muscles fire.
prereq: You need: physiological transducers and load cells, and the basic mechanics of force, pressure, velocity and acceleration.

sections.h3: Pedobarograph: pressure map of the foot

blocks.text: A pedobarograph measures pressure between the foot and the floor. A platform version has a flat sensor array; the patient walks across it. An insole version puts thin sensors inside the shoe and records many steps. Each sensor cell changes resistance or capacitance with load, and the instrument converts its voltage to pressure in kPa. Peak pressure is the highest cell pressure at an instant. Contact area is the number of loaded cells multiplied by one cell's area.

blocks.where: P is pressure in pascal (Pa); F is the force on one sensor cell in newton (N); A is that cell's area in square metre (m²). 1 kPa = 1000 Pa.

blocks.text: Calibration uses known loads applied over a known area. Put a known mass on the platform, or press the whole platform with a plate of known area, and record the output voltage at several loads. The load becomes a pressure P = mg / A in Pa, where m is the mass in kg, g is 9.81 m/s² and A is the loaded area in m². Fit a straight line to voltage against pressure; the slope is sensitivity in mV/kPa and the intercept is zero offset. If only the force is known and the area is not, report the slope in mV/N instead. A pressure map is not a force plate. A force plate gives total ground reaction force with load cells; a pedobarograph gives the spatial pattern of pressure.

Clinics use peak pressure to find hot spots under a diabetic foot and contact area to check load sharing. Insoles are trimmed where pressure is high. Platform data is clean but short; insole data is long but needs careful calibration.

One gait cycle starts when a foot touches the floor and ends when the same foot touches again. The stance phase is the time the foot is on the ground. The swing phase is the time the foot is in the air. In normal walking stance is about 60% of the cycle and swing about 40%; running changes this.

Step length is the distance between successive contacts of opposite feet. Stride length is the distance between successive contacts of the same foot. In a symmetric gait one stride is two steps. Cadence is steps per minute. Stride frequency is strides per second.

blocks.where: v is walking speed in m/s; L<sub>step</sub> is step length in m; c<sub>step</sub> is cadence in steps/s (cadence in steps/min divided by 60).

blocks.text: Speed also equals stride length times stride frequency. A walker with step length 0.7 m and cadence 120 steps/min has cadence 2 steps/s and speed 1.4 m/s. The figure shows a 1000 ms cycle with stance 0 to 600 ms and swing 600 to 1000 ms. Notice the cycle is 1.0 s, so stance is 0.6 s and swing is 0.4 s.

sections.h3: Limb position: angle, velocity and acceleration

blocks.text: A goniometer measures joint angle. A simple electrogoniometer has a potentiometer or strain gauge across the joint; its voltage changes as the angle changes. It is calibrated at known angles, for example 0° and 90°, to get a volts-per-degree slope.

An accelerometer measures acceleration. It also senses gravity, which on a limb is about 9.81 m/s², far larger than the movement signal. A gyroscope measures angular velocity. An inertial measurement unit (IMU) packs both.

Remove gravity before integrating. Using the sensor's orientation, find the component of gravity along its measuring axis, g<sub>axis</sub>, and subtract it: a<sub>motion</sub> = a<sub>measured</sub> − g<sub>axis</sub>. Only this motion term is integrated, once for velocity and twice for position. Integrating the raw reading gives a completely wrong velocity and position.
a<sub>motion</sub> = a<sub>measured</sub> − g<sub>axis</sub>,  v = Δx / Δt,  a = Δv / Δt
blocks.where: a<sub>measured</sub> is the raw accelerometer reading in m/s²; g<sub>axis</sub> is the part of gravity (9.81 m/s²) along the sensor's measuring axis, found from its orientation; a<sub>motion</sub> is the acceleration due to movement in m/s²; Δx is change in position in m; Δt is time interval in s; v is velocity in m/s; Δv is change in velocity in m/s; a is acceleration in m/s².

blocks.text: After gravity is removed, drift still comes from sensor bias and noise, and each integration adds more. So IMU position drifts. Camera systems avoid drift by tracking reflective markers on the limb. From marker positions x(t), velocity is v = Δx/Δt and acceleration is a = Δv/Δt.

Use goniometers for joint angle, IMUs for free walking outside a lab, and cameras for a reference in a gait lab. Sample fast enough: a walking gait has useful detail up to about 10 Hz to 20 Hz, so 100 samples/s gives margin.

examples.question: A walker has step length 0.7 m and cadence 120 steps/min. Find walking speed. If stance is 60% of a 1.0 s gait cycle, find stance and swing times. Assume symmetric gait.
steps: Cadence is given in steps/min; convert to steps/s: c = 120 / 60 = 2.0 steps/s.
Each step advances 0.7 m; speed = step length × cadence = 0.7 m × 2.0 steps/s = 1.4 m/s.
One gait cycle is 1.0 s. Stance fraction is 60% = 0.60. Stance time = 0.60 × 1.0 s = 0.60 s.
Swing time = cycle time − stance time = 1.0 s − 0.60 s = 0.40 s.
Check: stance + swing = 0.60 s + 0.40 s = 1.0 s.
examples.answer: Speed is 1.4 m/s (cadence 2.0 steps/s), stance time is 0.60 s and swing time is 0.40 s.
examples.check:
cadence_steps_min = 120
step_length = 0.7
cycle_time = 1.0
stance_fraction = 0.60
cadence_steps_s = cadence_steps_min / 60
speed = step_length * cadence_steps_s
stance_time = stance_fraction * cycle_time
swing_time = cycle_time - stance_time
print(f'{cadence_steps_s:.1f}')
print(f'{speed:.1f}')
print(f'{stance_time:.1f}')
print(f'{swing_time:.1f}')

examples.question: A pedobarograph platform has square sensor cells 5 mm on a side. Under the heel of a standing 70 kg patient the most loaded cell carries 12.5 N, and 480 cells are loaded in all. Find the peak pressure, the contact area and the mean pressure under the foot. Take g = 9.81 m/s².
steps: Cell area A = 5 mm × 5 mm = 25 mm² = 25 × 10⁻⁶ m² = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ m².
Peak pressure = F ÷ A = 12.5 N ÷ 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ m² = 500,000 Pa = 500 kPa.
Contact area = 480 × 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ m² = 0.012 m², that is 120 cm².
Body weight = m g = 70 × 9.81 = 686.7 N. Mean pressure = 686.7 N ÷ 0.012 m² = 57,225 Pa = 57.2 kPa.
Check: the peak cell is about 9 times the mean (500 ÷ 57.2 = 8.7), the hot spot a clinician looks for under the heel.
examples.answer: Peak pressure 500 kPa, contact area 0.012 m² (120 cm²) and mean pressure 57.2 kPa.

traps: Cadence is steps/min, not strides/min. One stride is two steps.
Step length is not stride length; for a symmetric gait stride length = 2 × step length.
Pressure is force per area. Peak pressure is not total force; a small area gives high pressure with modest force.
In a gait cycle, stance plus swing = 100%. Normal walking is about 60% stance and 40% swing, not 50/50.
Inertial sensor position comes from double integration and drifts; one clean short trial does not prove long-term accuracy.

quiz.a: An instrument that maps pressure between the foot and the floor using a sensor platform or an in-shoe insole.

quiz.q: Why must a pressure insole be calibrated before use?
quiz.a: Sensor output voltage changes with temperature, wear and mounting. Calibration converts voltage to kPa and removes zero offset.

quiz.q: A walker has step length 0.6 m and cadence 110 steps/min. Find speed and stride length. Assume symmetric gait.
quiz.a: Cadence = 110/60 = 1.833 steps/s. Speed = 0.6 × 1.833 = 1.1 m/s. Stride length = 2 × 0.6 = 1.2 m.

quiz.q: Stance is 65% of a 1.2 s gait cycle. Find stance and swing times. What happens to swing time if cadence rises but stance fraction stays 65%?
quiz.a: Stance = 0.65 × 1.2 = 0.78 s. Swing = 1.2 − 0.78 = 0.42 s. If cadence rises, cycle time falls, so both stance and swing times fall; swing = 0.35 × cycle time.

quiz.q: Give one advantage of a goniometer and one advantage of an IMU for limb position.
quiz.a: A goniometer gives direct joint angle with simple electronics. An IMU is wearable and works outside the lab. The gyroscope inside the IMU gives orientation, which allows gravity to be removed from the accelerometer reading and so slows position drift. It cannot remove sensor bias, so drift still grows with time.

quiz.q: Why does an accelerometer alone give poor limb position over 1 minute?
quiz.a: First, gravity must be removed: a<sub>motion</sub> = a<sub>measured</sub> − g<sub>axis</sub>, where g<sub>axis</sub> is the gravity component along the sensor axis, about 9.81 m/s². A raw reading at rest is mostly gravity, not motion, so integrating it directly is meaningless. Even after removal, position needs double integration, so constant offset and noise integrate into growing velocity error, then into position drift.
Cadence is steps per minute. Stride length is the distance between successive contacts of the same foot; one stride is two steps.

quiz.q: A pressure cell of area 0.0004 m² carries 30 N. Find pressure in kPa.

beyond: Not for the exam. Wearable pressure insoles now stream data over Bluetooth to phones, and machine-learning models classify gait from a few steps. Inertial sensors in phones can estimate step count and walking speed. Research combines pressure maps with video markers to model joint loading. Search terms: plantar pressure mapping, inertial gait analysis, markerless motion capture.
